turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. ChatGPT. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hello, Doctor. It’s, uh... it’s a bit of a long story, I suppose, but I'll try to explain how this all came about. You see, since I’m not working right now—just taking some time away from the workforce, you know, so I'm around the house a lot more these days—my wife and I are obviously spending a lot of time together. And she’s wonderful, she really is, she handles so much of the family logistics and keeps everything running. 

Lately, she’s been helping out my cousin quite a bit. My cousin has all these different things going on, and he needs rides here and there, and my wife is the one coordinating all of his schedule. So... what really brought me in today, what finally made her sit me down and say I need to talk to a doctor, is that she’ll be standing right there in the kitchen or the living room, telling me all about my cousin’s appointments or who is giving him rides on what day. And I’m looking right at her. I mean, I'm making eye contact, I'm nodding, I genuinely think I'm paying full attention to her. But then, literally a minute later, I realize I didn’t actually take in half of what she said. 

The words just sort of... evaporate. And she gets so frustrated with me, understandably, because she thinks I don't care or that I'm just ignoring her, but I'm really not trying to. I just sit there realizing I have absolutely no idea what time she just said the ride was, or which doctor he's seeing, and it's just causing a lot of friction between us because it happens all the time.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly states that when his wife speaks directly to him, he looks at her and nods but fails to take in what she is saying, indicating difficulty listening when spoken to directly.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have similar trouble paying attention or following through when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it’s funny you ask that, Doctor, because my wife actually asked me the exact same thing the other day when she was getting so frustrated with me. And... when I really sat down and thought about it, going all the way back, the answer is yes. Absolutely. 

I mean, even way back in grade school—this would be well before I was 12, probably starting around third or fourth grade, maybe even earlier—I remember my parents coming home from those parent-teacher conferences. It was always, and I mean always, the exact same story. The teachers would sit them down and say, 'He’s a very bright boy, he really is, he has so much potential.' But then they'd sigh and say that I was just constantly daydreaming. I’d be staring out the classroom window at the trees or the playground, just completely lost in my own little world, thinking about who knows what, while everyone else was focused on the lesson. 

And the follow-through... oh boy. I would actually do my homework at home, well, most of the time anyway, but then I'd just leave it sitting right there inside my desk at school. You know those old wooden desks with the open cubby part underneath? My papers would just get shoved in there and completely forgotten. The teachers were always having to walk over, tap on my shoulder, and give me these constant reminders just to finish the regular classwork that was sitting right in front of my face. So, yes, it’s definitely not a new thing, it’s just... it's always been a part of how I operate, I suppose, even as a little kid. It just looks a little different now that I'm a grown man forgetting about my cousin's doctor appointments instead of my math worksheets.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes constantly daydreaming and losing focus during lessons as a child.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient reports needing constant reminders to finish classwork and failing to turn in completed homework.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient mentions being distracted by looking out the classroom window at the trees or playground.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient notes a history of forgetting homework in their desk and currently forgetting appointments.
